A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CTC-DRO research, with readable text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. Content can be matched across relocation and renumbering. Differences in reported experimental settings require caution when comparing scores directly.

before.justification: v1 reports original multilingual ASR experiments with MMS and XLS-R, including balanced and unbalanced training, component ablations, and language-specific appendix results.

after.justification: v3 reports original ASR results, including revised main comparisons and additional normalization, batch-duration, four-seed, WER, and 18-language experiments.

M1.justification: The core length-matched batching and smoothed group-weight update remain. However, line 21 changes from a weighted average batch loss in v1 Algorithm 2 to a weighted sum in v3 Algorithm 1, removing division by batch size. This changes the stated loss used for model-parameter updates; the PDFs do not establish whether it corrects documentation or changes implementation.

E1.justification: The original five six-language sets and their balanced/unbalanced coverage remain. v3 adds an 18-language evaluation under both data regimes, including Bashkort, Burmese, French, Guarani, and Swati, which were absent from v1's evaluated sets (Appendix H, Table 17). This substantially extends joint multilingual coverage within the same ASR benchmark.

E2.justification: The main comparator identities remain the CTC baseline and group DRO, abbreviated Base and GDRO in v3. Appendix G, Table 16 additionally evaluates frame-normalized and target-normalized group DRO alternatives. v1 mentions unsuccessful normalization experiments but does not report these comparator results.

E3.justification: v3 Section 4 explicitly adds length-matched batching to the stated baseline recipe while retaining the original sampler for group DRO. New evaluation designs include WER scoring on set 4 and a 23-versus-46-second batch-duration comparison on set 5. The main data splits, 40-epoch budget, and 16-batch gradient accumulation remain; the PDFs do not identify which earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablation and XLS-R group-weight analysis, v3 adds normalization comparisons, batch-duration sensitivity, four-seed robustness, best-language tradeoff analysis, and scalability tests. Additional MMS weight trajectories test whether the stability finding extends across models and language sets (Appendices F–H).

E5.justification: v1 provides performance point estimates without run-count or performance-uncertainty reporting; its standard deviations describe dataset statistics. v3 Table 15 reports four-seed means, standard deviations, differences, and win counts for sets 1 and 3. Appendix F.5 additionally introduces paired t-tests and p-values for best-language comparisons across settings.

E6.justification: Main results change substantially: balanced set 1 XLS-R baseline/CTC-DRO worst-language CER changes from 187.9/64.0 in v1 Table 2 to 64.9/57.6 in v3 Table 1. These revised results do not establish a controlled cross-version performance gain given the differing procedure descriptions. Numerous results are added, including Table 15's worse mean worst-language CER for set 3 XLS-R with CTC-DRO: 34.7 versus baseline 33.2.

T1.justification: v3 Section 3.2 extends the existing Lagrangian argument rather than introducing a new theory. It replaces v1's abbreviated proportionality step with equalities, explicitly assumes positive group weights, invokes complementary slackness, and derives the normalized interior solution in Equations 14–17. This is a substantive but localized mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The central contribution and qualitative superiority claim remain. The abstract and introduction reduce the advertised maximum worst-language/average error reductions from 65.9%/47.7% to 47.1%/32.9%. The conclusion also broadens suggested applicability from other sequence tasks to settings with group-level losses, while presenting these extensions as possibilities.

C2.justification: v3 adds substantive explanations of normalization's effects on relative gradients, CER–WER disagreement, batch-duration sensitivity, and scalability tradeoffs. It newly interprets statistical tests as showing no significant best-language degradation. Conversely, the relocated impact statement removes v1's specific warning that CER may not reflect transcript usefulness, although general deployment cautions remain.

D1.justification: v3 supplies selected hyperparameters, the learning rate of 10^-4, per-set batch durations, A6000 hardware, training times, and an approximate overall compute budget. These substantially expand reproducibility information. Its introduction supplies a repository link and states that code and models are public, replacing v1's release promise, although Appendix B still contains future-release wording.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands positioning through comparisons with auxiliary CTC objectives, conditional adapters, other DRO variants, and reinforcement-learning approaches, citing Chen et al. (2023), Lu et al. (2024), Lokhande et al. (2022), and Tjandra et al. (2018). It also adds motivation concerning CTC versus autoregressive ASR. The original first-successful-robust-optimization novelty claim remains.

P1.justification: The main section sequence remains, but supporting material is substantially reorganized: the group DRO algorithm, dataset overview, CER definition, and impact statement move into dedicated appendices. The objective/update exposition is reordered, motivation and related-work prose expand, and the former compact appendices become a structured development-results, test-results, and analysis narrative.

P2.justification: v3 changes the main text from two columns to one, rearranges retained tables into side-by-side blocks, and adds hyperparameter columns to the main result tables. It retains the original plots while adding two MMS weight-trajectory figures and numerous development, robustness, normalization, scaling, and timing tables. These are substantial display and layout changes beyond numerical updates.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the method's reliability and limits: normalization comparisons, batch-duration tests, four-seed results, broader language coverage, and measured training costs address questions left unresolved by v1's basic comparisons and ablations. Reproducibility details also improve considerably. The added evidence exposes mixed outcomes, including the set 3 XLS-R seed reversal. Some overstatement remains—the conclusion still describes LID improvements in almost all cases despite Section 5 reporting seven of fourteen—but the gains in evaluability and empirical support outweigh these residual weaknesses.
